entry.title: Part 2: From MCP to Natural Language: SAP Integration Suite and Joule Work Desktop
entry.content:
Hi everyone, and welcome to Part 2!

In Part 1, we started with an existing Business Partner (A2X) OData API, brought it into SAP Integration Suite as an API artifact, exposed selected capabilities through an MCP Server on Integration Cell, and published the result through Developer Hub.

Now comes the part that originally made this experiment interesting to me.

What happens when the user stops thinking about APIs and simply expresses what they want in natural language?

Our complete architecture now looks like this:

Let's connect JWD and try it.

 

 

Step 1: Connect Joule Work Desktop as the MCP client

 
If you haven't completed the MCP Server and Developer Hub setup yet, start with Part 1: From OData to MCP.

Now we can finally connect the client.

For this demo, I used Joule Work Desktop (JWD) as the MCP client and configured the connection using the MCP endpoint and OAuth information obtained through Developer Hub.

Conceptually, we have now completed the entire architecture:

Joule Work Desktop
        │
       MCP
        ▼
SAP Integration Suite
        │
   MCP Server
        │
Integration Cell Runtime
        │
      OData
        ▼
Business Partner API

Once the connector appeared as available in JWD, the configuration was behind us and I was ready to test the complete flow from the user's perspective using natural language.

This is where things become much more interesting.

Step 2: Ask the first natural-language question

Now comes the fun part.

The prompts in this example are intentionally simple.

I'm not trying to demonstrate advanced prompt engineering or prescribe a specific output format. Instead, I want to see how naturally a user can express an intent when the underlying enterprise capability is exposed through MCP.

In a production scenario, prompts could certainly be more explicit about scope, output format, constraints, and expected behaviour. For this experiment, however, I've deliberately kept them conversational.

Instead of testing the integration using API terminology, I ask JWD:

Find business partners in Germany and show me their names and cities.

What's interesting is what I didn't have to specify:

  • an OData endpoint;
  • an entity name;
  • query parameters;
  • filter syntax; or
  • a response structure.

I simply described what I wanted.

That is a very different consumption experience from working directly with an API.

But underneath that simple sentence, we are still using the Business Partner capability that we started with in Part 1.

Step 3: Continue the same conversation

The next test is deliberately not another independent API request.

I simply continue:

Tell me more about the first one, including its address and contact information.

The interesting phrase here is:

“the first one”

From the user's perspective, this is a continuation of the conversation.

There is no need to copy a Business Partner identifier from one result, work out another API operation, and construct another technical request.

The user simply expresses the next intent in the conversation.

Step 4: Move from data retrieval to business intent

Finally, I take it one step further:

Summarize what we know about this business partner in a way that would be useful before a customer call.

The progression now looks like this:

1. Find enterprise data
             │
             ▼
2. Continue conversationally
             │
             ▼
3. Turn the retrieved information
   into a user-oriented response

This is the point where, for me, the scenario becomes more interesting than simply saying “an LLM can call an API.”

We're starting with existing enterprise capabilities and changing how a user can interact with them.

Step 5: What just happened?

 
Let's return to the architecture one more time:

And this brings us back to the main point of the experiment:

The Business Partner API didn't have to become conversational.

It remains an enterprise API.

The MCP Server makes selected capabilities available through MCP, while SAP Integration Suite provides the runtime layer between the MCP consumer and the underlying enterprise service.

You can find more detail about this architecture in the SAP Integration Suite MCP documentation.

What I learned

A few things stood out to me while putting this scenario together.

1. Existing APIs become more valuable, not less

MCP doesn't mean replacing our existing REST or OData APIs.

In this scenario, the Business Partner API remains the underlying business capability. What changes is the way that capability can be exposed and consumed.

That gives our existing API investments another potential class of consumer: AI clients and agents.

2. The user experience changes dramatically

Compare the traditional API consumption process:

Understand the API
        ↓
Understand the data model
        ↓
Construct the request
        ↓
Process the response

with:

Find business partners in Germany and show me their names and cities.

The underlying business capability can remain the same while the consumer experience becomes completely different.

3. MCP authentication and backend authentication are different concerns

 

This became especially clear while building the demo.

On one side, JWD authenticates as an MCP consumer.

On the other side, Integration Suite has to authenticate when invoking the backend Business Partner API.

JWD
 │
 │ MCP authentication
 ▼
SAP Integration Suite
 │
 │ Backend authentication
 ▼
Business Partner API

Keeping these two concerns separate made the architecture, and the troubleshooting, much clearer.

4. Developer Hub was the missing piece for my JWD connection

 

My initial attempt focused too much on creating credentials directly.

The successful path was:

Deploy → Publish through Developer Hub → Subscribe → Retrieve credentials → Connect JWD

Once I followed that consumption model, the pieces came together.

Closing thoughts

For me, this is where MCP starts to get really interesting.

The exciting part isn't that an AI client can execute an HTTP request. It's that we can take business capabilities that already exist, selectively expose them through MCP, and let users interact with those capabilities in terms of intent rather than API implementation.

The Business Partner API remains an API.

What changed is how the capability is discovered, invoked, and experienced by the user.

And that raises an interesting question for integration architects:

As AI clients become another consumer of enterprise capabilities, how should we design, expose, secure, and govern the APIs behind them?

I'd love to hear how others are exploring MCP in their own integration scenarios. If you've tried connecting MCP clients to SAP Integration Suite, or have a different approach to exposing enterprise APIs to AI clients, please share your experience, questions, or lessons learned in the comments below. Let's learn from each other!

Further reading

  • Model Context Protocol (MCP) in SAP Integration Suite
  • Build and Govern MCP Servers with SAP Integration Suite
  • Create an MCP Server for Enterprise AI Agents
  • Create a Reusable API Artifact
  • Discover and Publish MCP Servers from SAP Integration Suite
  • SAP Business Accelerator Hub

entry.title: Joule A2A: MCP Gateway to S/4HANA with Principal Propagation
entry.content:
In a previous post we looked at connecting a custom A2A agent to S/4HANA Public Cloud with full principal propagation. But that approach comes with some drawbacks: hooking up individual APIs doesn't scale well, and it's hard to enforce governance. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for exposing tools and data to AI agents in a uniform way, and it's quickly becoming the common language between agents and enterprise systems. SAP's reference architecture for Agents and MCP positions Integration Suite as an MCP Gateway to safeguard traffic to enterprise systems — so this post extends the example to route a BTP-based agent through that gateway, still from customer-managed Joule.

Note: This post covers Customer-Managed Joule.

Scenario

We have an A2A-capable agent connected to Joule (customer-managed), with a destination that hands the Joule user's token to the agent on each A2A request. To reach S/4HANA Public Cloud, that agent now goes through the MCP Gateway: Integration Suite points its gateway at an S/4HANA OData service via a destination, the selected endpoints become MCP tools, and it all runs on Integration Cell. The user identity is propagated the whole way — from Joule, through the custom agent, through the MCP Gateway, into S/4HANA — so the backend call runs as the real user. And because the gateway sits on Integration Suite, we inherit the API Management controls we already know: additional authentication and authorization on top, plus IP filtering, rate limiting and quotas where we need them.

This matters because many customers have built their agents in an A2A manner, and their API policy often restricts them to endorsed architectures only.

Prerequisites

  • A working A2A agent and destination setup, as described in the principal propagation post
  • An S/4HANA Public Cloud system
  • Integration Suite, Enhanced Edition (only that Edition contains the MCP Gateway)

Step 1: Trust the Integration Suite subaccount in S/4

The very first step diverges from the previous post: the trust setup. Last time we configured S/4 to trust the destination certificate of the agent's subaccount. This time the piece that resolves the SAML Bearer assertion is the destination service of the subaccount where Integration Suite lives — and that is a different subaccount, with a different signing certificate (at least in my case). So we repeat the communication setup against that subaccount.

Concretely, in your Integration Suite subaccount go to Connectivity → Destinations → Download Trust and grab the .pem. It is a self-signed cert whose subject looks like cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/<subaccount-id> with OU=CP Destination Configuration — this is the destination-service signing certificate.

Then, exactly as in the principal propagation post, set up a communication user, a communication system and a communication arrangement (SAP_COM_0008 for Business Partner) in S/4 — but upload this certificate under the communication system's OAuth 2.0 Identity Provider, and copy its subject CN into the Provider Name field.

Note: if the trust is missing or points at the wrong subaccount, the SAML exchange later fails with a very explicit "There is no trust between entities … in client 100". That message contains the subaccount ID it actually saw, which makes it easy to tell that you trusted the wrong one.

Step 2: Create the S/4HANA SAML Bearer destination in the IS subaccount

Next, create an HTTP destination toward S/4HANA in the subaccount where Integration Suite resides. This is the same OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion destination as in the previous post — the MCP server will use it as its target. The important properties:

Name=S4_MCP_GATEWAY_TEST
Type=HTTP
ProxyType=Internet
Authentication=OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion
URL=https://my3xxxxx-api.s4hana.cloud.sap
Audience=https://my3xxxxx.s4hana.cloud.sap
Token Service URL=https://my3xxxxx-api.s4hana.cloud.sap/sap/bc/sec/oauth2/token
Client Key / Token Service User=<the comm user from step 1>
authnContextClassRef=urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:X509
userIdSource=mail
nameIdFormat=urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:emailAddress

# additional properties
x_user_token.jwks_uri=https://<your-ias-tenant>/oauth2/certs
IntegrationCell.Include=true

Two things that are easy to miss:

  • x_user_token.jwks_uri points at the IAS tenant so the destination service can validate the forwarded end-user token and build the SAML assertion for the real user. Without it, it silently falls back to a technical-user assertion and propagation breaks.
  • IntegrationCell.Include=true is a label on the destination. Without it the destination simply won't appear in the MCP Server wizard's dropdown at all.

Step 3: Build the MCP server in Integration Suite

Now the new part. In Design → Integrations and APIs, create an integration package to hold the artifact.

Inside the package, add an MCP Server artifact. The wizard's first step asks for the source type — pick HTTP Endpoint with OpenAPI Specification:

In the next step, point it at the S4_MCP_GATEWAY_TEST destination with a relative URL of /sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER, give it a name and an MCP Path (e.g. /s4_bp_mcp), and leave the runtime profile on Integration Cell:

Skip the AI spec generation. Once the artifact exists, open its MCP Configuration → Source tab and hit Edit API Specification to supply the spec:

Import the OpenAPI/EDMX of the Business Partner service — you can download it from the SAP Business Accelerator Hub, or just pull the live $metadata from your own system:

On the Tools tab, select the operations you want to expose; each one becomes an MCP tool. I started with a single GET A_BusinessPartner → the tool get_A_BusinessPartner. Keep it small; the model routes better with fewer, well-described tools:

The tricky part is the inbound security — this is where the whole principal-propagation story lives. On the Policies tab every MCP server has a mandatory Authentication and Authorization policy, so we look at both.

Authentication

The Authentication policy decides which tokens the gateway trusts. By default an MCP server validates tokens issued through the Integration Suite subaccount's own XSUAA / the IdP configured there. That default path is enough for a client like Joule Work Desktop, which runs its own user-token fetch flow against that trusted authorization server when you add the connector — so the end-user identity is already there, you don't configure anything extra on the gateway.

Our case is different: the token doesn't come from a JWD connector, it's the JWT our A2A agent forwards from Joule, issued by our IAS tenant — and a raw token from that issuer is rejected by the default policy with 401 invalidToken because the gateway doesn't trust it yet.

The fix is to switch the Authentication policy to External OAuth (OIDC) and point it at our IAS tenant. Even though this feels a bit strange — our IAS tenant is treated as an "external" OAuth provider here — the "internal" option is the subaccount's XSUAA, which may well itself be configured to redirect logins to exactly that same IAS. So "external" just means: validate the token directly against the IAS tenant, by its own issuer and keys.

Once External OAuth is selected, there are four fields to fill:

Field Value

Well-Known URLhttps://<ias-tenant>/.well-known/openid-configuration
Audiencethe aud of the token the client actually sends (see the gotcha below)
ClientID Key${authn.oidc.jwt.azp}
UserInfo Key${authn.oidc.jwt.mail}

What these actually do: the Well-Known URL tells the gateway which IAS tenant to trust — it discovers the issuer and the signing keys from there, and validates every incoming token's signature against them. The Audience is the gateway saying "I only accept tokens that were actually meant for this application" — it's matched against the token's aud claim. ClientID Key and UserInfo Key are expressions that tell the gateway which claims carry the calling client's ID (azp) and the end user's identity (mail) — the latter being exactly the identity that gets propagated downstream.

The Audience is the one that'll bite you. Our destination maps userIdSource=mail, and the token that eventually arrives is the one Joule forwarded — i.e. after its app-to-app exchange — so its aud is the Custom Agent App client ID, not the login app you used to get a test token. You find that client ID in your IAS admin console under Applications → your Custom Agent App → Client ID (it's the same value that your agent already validates as its IAS_AUDIENCE). If you set the policy audience to the wrong app, the real Joule token is rejected with 401 invalidToken even though everything else is correct. You can also list multiple audiences comma-separated, or leave it empty to skip audience validation entirely while debugging.

If authentication is not configured correctly, the gateway rejects the call before it ever reaches your backend — a decoded IAS token that doesn't match issuer/audience comes back as:

{ "error": { "code": "invalidToken", "message": "Unable to authenticate user, invalid token" } }

(HTTP 401)

Authorization

The second mandatory policy is Authorization — and this is where it helps to understand how an IAS token is built, because it is fundamentally different from the XSUAA token you may be used to.

An XSUAA access token carries a scope claim (things like myapp.Read, API.invoke), and the default Authorization policy checks exactly that: does the token contain the required scope? An IAS token has no scope claim at all. IAS is an identity provider — it answers "who are you", not "what may you do"; the actual authorization is expected to happen in the target system (the user's S/4 roles, in our case). A decoded IAS user token has mail, sub, azp — but nothing a scope-based policy can match on.

What an IAS token does carry, because it came through Joule's app-to-app exchange, is the ias_apis claim — a list of the exposed APIs the user is allowed to call:

{
  "iss": "https://<ias-tenant>",
  "aud": "<custom-agent-app client id>",
  "azp": "<proxy-app client id>",
  "mail": "felix.bartler@sap.com",
  "ias_apis": ["a2a_custom_agent_app_api"]
}

So the configuration change versus the XSUAA default is: don't check a scope claim, check the ias_apis list instead. Point the Authorization policy's Scope Key at ias_apis and set the expected value to our exposed API:

Authorization field Value

Authorization TypeOAuth Scope OR Developer Key
Scope Keyias_apis
Scopea2a_custom_agent_app_api

The policy then checks whether the ias_apis list contains a2a_custom_agent_app_api — which doubles as a useful access gate: it enforces, right at the gateway, that only users entitled to this agent's exposed API can call it at all.

If authorization is wrong — e.g. the policy still checks scope, which an IAS token doesn't have — the gateway authenticates the user fine but then refuses the operation:

{ "error": { "code": "forbidden", "message": "User doesn't have the authorization to perform this operation" } }

(HTTP 403)

With both policies right, the gateway accepts the real Joule user token, validates it against IAS, reads mail, and forwards the identity to the destination.

Deploy MCP Server

Finally Deploy onto the Integration Cell runtime, and once the Runtime Status reads STARTED the MCP URL is live:

We've basically turned an OData endpoint into a proper MCP Server — with a curated list of tools — and put an auth layer in front of it that enforces principal propagation. Let's test it:

Testing the gateway with curl

Before touching any agent code, it's worth proving the gateway end to end in isolation — exactly like the SAML dry-run in the previous post. MCP over Streamable HTTP is just JSON-RPC over HTTP, so three curl calls do it: initialize (which returns an mcp-session-id response header you must echo back), notifications/initialized, then tools/call.

# USER_JWT = a REAL Joule-forwarded token (see the caveat below), MCP_URL = the deployed MCP server URL

# 1) initialize — grab the mcp-session-id straight from the response header
SID=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%header{mcp-session-id}' -X POST "$MCP_URL" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_JWT" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"curl","version":"1.0"}}}')

# 2) say "initialized"
curl -s -o /dev/null -X POST "$MCP_URL" -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_JWT" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" -H "mcp-session-id: $SID" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/initialized"}'

# 3) call the tool as the user (note: OData options without `$`, select is an ARRAY)
curl -s -X POST "$MCP_URL" -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_JWT" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" -H "mcp-session-id: $SID" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_A_BusinessPartner","arguments":{"top":3,"select":["BusinessPartner","BusinessPartnerName"]}}}'

This is the fastest feedback loop for getting the two policies right — the error you get back tells you exactly which stage failed: 401 invalidToken = authentication (issuer/audience), 403 forbidden = authorization (scope/ias_apis), real OData rows = success.

Getting a token that actually works for the test. A plain IAS password grant gives you a token audienced for the login app and without ias_apis, so it fails both audience and authorization — it is not a stand-in for what Joule sends. You have two options to get a realistic token:

  1. Reproduce the app-to-app exchange yourself. This is exactly what Joule does internally: take the user token and exchange it (via the jwt-bearer grant against your IAS, using the proxy app's client credentials and the proxy-to-target dependency) into a token audienced for the Custom Agent App — which then carries ias_apis. If you own the proxy app's credentials, this is the clean, scriptable way and the one I'd recommend for a proper test harness.
  2. Capture a real one. Quicker for a one-off: temporarily log the raw Authorization header in your agent, prompt Joule once, and copy the forwarded JWT out of the logs.

Step 4: The Python agent that calls the MCP gateway

The change on the agent side is small and local: the one place that used to call the destination service and S/4 directly (s4_client.py in the previous post) is replaced by a small MCP client. Everything else — the LangGraph tool, the executor, the IAS middleware on the agent's own inbound endpoint — stays as it was.

The MCP client uses Streamable-HTTP JSON-RPC to call the MCP Gateway. This is part of the standard of MCP - and one could also use a SDK. We do 3 calls: initialize (which hands back an mcp-session-id response header you carry on every following request), notifications/initialized, and tools/call:

# mcp_client.py (abridged)
def call_business_partner_api(user_jwt, top=10, select=None, filter_expr=None, ...):
    session_id = _open_session(user_jwt)        # initialize -> mcp-session-id
    r = requests.post(
        MCP_URL,
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {user_jwt}",   # <-- the whole trick
            "Accept": "application/json, text/event-stream",
            "mcp-session-id": session_id,
        },
        json={
            "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "tools/call",
            "params": {
                "name": "get_A_BusinessPartner",
                "arguments": {"top": top, "select": [...]},   # OData options, no `$`, select is an array
            },
        },
    )
    # tool output comes back as result.content[0].text (JSON string of the OData payload)

The user_jwt it forwards is the exact same token the agent already extracts from the inbound A2A request — unchanged from the previous post:

# agent_executor.py — the token comes straight from the Authorization header Joule sent
auth = context._call_context.state.get("headers", {}).get("authorization", "")
user_jwt = auth[len("bearer "):] if auth.lower().startswith("bearer ") else None
# ... threaded down to the tool, which puts it on the MCP call as Authorization: Bearer

The key point: the agent needs no credentials of its own for the backend. No client secret, no destination binding to S/4 — just the MCP_URL of the deployed gateway. It takes the user's token and passes it on; IAS, the gateway and the destination service do the rest. (The agent's own inbound A2A endpoint is still protected by the IAS middleware exactly as before.)

Two details are worth knowing when calling an Integration-Suite-generated tool: the handshake is session-based (echo the mcp-session-id header after initialize), and the generated tool schema uses OData options without the leading $, with select/expand/orderby as arrays of strings — pass a comma-separated string and the call fails schema validation.

Test in Joule

Deploy the agent, point Joule's agent destination at it, and prompt it — e.g. "show me business partners that start with I". The full chain runs: the agent forwards the user's token to the gateway, the gateway validates it against IAS, propagates the signed-in user through the SAML Bearer destination, and S/4HANA returns exactly the records that user is authorized to see, rendered as a table in the conversation:

This is the point of the whole exercise: the data comes back scoped to the real signed-in user, propagated all the way from Joule to S/4HANA — exactly the behaviour we wanted. And because it now runs through the gateway, we can also see it happen: in Integration Suite under Monitor → Integrations and APIs → Monitor Message Processing (with the Integration Cell runtime selected), each prompt shows up as a BusinessPartnerMCP entry of type MCP Server, status Completed. That's the proof the call actually traversed the MCP gateway rather than some direct backchannel — and the governance, tracing and policy enforcement that come with it apply to every call.

Conclusion

Looks good. We have the full flow in place and can use the MCP Gateway for our A2A Agents. Hope you found this insightful.

The full code is on GitHub under a2a_pp_mcp_gateway/.

This post is part of the Joule A2A series:

  • Connect code-based agents into Joule
  • Secure code-based agents with IAS
  • Handling multi-turn conversations
  • Building custom Joule capabilities: message types in practice
  • Propagate the user identity from Joule into S/4HANA
  • MCP Gateway to S/4HANA with Principal Propagation (this post)

entry.title: Best Practices Pipeline for Cloud Integration: Working with Parties
entry.content:
You like to use parties in combination with the Pipeline for Cloud Integration. Parties need to be taken into consideration for different use cases and configuration options. So, this blog post describes how to generally setup your configuration scenarios when using parties.

Note: For exchanging IDoc messages, parties are heavily used when your partner type is not LS. Covering IDocs would exceed the scope of this blog post. For this, I would refer to Enhanced IDoc inbound support for Cloud Integration Pipeline where I describe how to setup IDoc inbound scenarios depending on the sender and (virtual) receiver partner type.

So, let's stick here to the more generic usage of parties. In general, we decided to go for a simplified way how to support parties in the Pipeline for Cloud Integration. We simply combine the party name and  the system name by separating both parts using a period, ".", e.g., PartyA.XYZ. See Scenarios with Sender Party or Receiver Party.

The combined party and system can then be used in different configurations such as:

  • In your alternative partner to determine the partner ID representing the configuration scenario.
  • For sender-specific inbound conversion.
  • In the XSLT to determine the receivers (with party).
  • For P2P, to determine the receiver (with party).
  • For the generic XI/IDoc outbound processing, to define the XI/IDoc connection and scenario settings.

So, here some rules:

  • In your scenario-specific integration flow, maintain the header SAP_Sender as combined sender party and sender system name as described above.
  • For XI inbound scenarios, this is automatically done. Here, the generic XI inbound processing flow creates the header SAP_Sender as a combination of the header SapSenderParty and SapSenderService provided by the XI sender adapter.
  • To determine the configuration scenario, maintain the alternative partner of the partner ID in the Partner Directory accordingly. In this case, define the agency as the combined sender party and sender system name.
  • For receiver parties, maintain the receiver service name in the XSLT to determine the receivers as combined receiver party and receiver system name.
  • For the Point-to-Point pattern, maintain the value of the string parameter receiverDetermination as combined receiver party and receiver system name.
  • For some configuration options, you need to add the combined party name and system name as suffix to the corresponding string parameter.

In message monitoring, you will notice the following:

  • If the header SAP_Sender contains a party, the header SAP_SenderParty is created holding the party name. Furthermore, the value of the header SAP_Sender is split up defining the custom header properties SenderParty and SenderSystem, which are then displayed in the message processing log.
  • If the header SAP_Receiver contains a party, the header SAP_ReceiverParty is created holding the party name. Furthermore, the value of the header SAP_Receiver is split up defining the custom header properties ReceiverParty and ReceiverSystem, which are then displayed in the message processing log.

Let's take a look at some examples.

XI inbound scenario

In this use case, we focus on the inbound side. This is a scenario where we send XI messages to the pipeline whereas the XI header contains both party and system.

We use landscape staging, and would like to test our scenario on the QA landscape. First of all, we need to define a business system alias for the sender system, here BC_02D_S1. In the alternative partner of the alias, we map the actual business system name, here BS_02D_S1Q for the QA landscape, to the alias. We do the same for the second sender, here alias BC_02D_S2 with actual business system name BS_02D_S2Q.

As said, both senders have a party. So, in the alternative partner of the partner ID representing the configuration scenario, we need to define the agency as combination of the party name and the system alias name. In our case BuyerA.BC_02D_S1 and BuyerB.BC_02D_S2, respectively. Scheme of the alternative partner is the sender interface name, ID is the sender interface namespace.

An inbound conversion is needed after the message has been received by the pipeline. In our case, the inbound conversion should be sender-specific. So, for each of the sender we define a string parameter InboundConversionEndpoint with suffix as combined party and sender system alias, here InboundConversionEndpoint_BuyerA.BC_02D_S1 and InboundConversionEndpoint_BuyerB.BC_02D_S2, respectively. As value, we enter the ProcessDirect endpoint of the inbound conversion flows that carry out the conversion.

I switched on the trace for the generic XI inbound processing flow. In the trace, you can see the payload of the incoming message including XI header. So, here you can see that the XI header contains the sender party BuyerA and the sender service BS_02D_S1Q.

In the message monitoring, you can see that the SAP_Sender (Sender in the Properties) is a combination of the party and the business system name, here BuyerA.BS_02D_S1Q. The custom header properties show the sender alias, sender system and sender party information. During runtime, the sender system alias BC_02D_S1 is determined based on the sender business system name BS_02D_S1Q and the landscape stage QA (via the alternative parner of the system alias). The combined party and sender system alias BuyerA.BC_02D_S1 is then used to determine the configuration scenario (via the alternative parner of the configuration scenario). Once, the configuration scenario has been determined, the other parameters are read from the Partner Directory to dynamically define how the message processing behaves.

Configure XI/IDoc Outbound

In this use case, we focus on the outbound side. This is a scenario where we use the generic XI and IDoc outbound processing flows to configure the XI and IDoc receiver adapters and scenario parameters. Here, the receivers contain party.

Again, we use landscape staging. First of all, we need to define a business system alias for the receiver system, here BC_02L_R1. In the alternative partner of the alias, we map the actual business system name, here BS_02L_R1Q for the QA landscape, to the alias.

This is a content-based router pattern. So, we create an XSLT mapping to determine the receivers and upload it to the Binary Parameters of the configuration scenario with ID receiverDetermination.

The XSLT looks as follows. As you can see, we either route a message to the one party or the other. In our case for both parties, the system is the same. However, they can also differ. In our case, the service is defined as combined party and receiver system alias, so either PRTY_02L_Bronze.BC_02L_R1 or PRTY_02L_Copper.BC_02L_R1. Note: in the XSLT we always use the alias, so we can use the same XSLT in each landscape stage.

To configure the XI and IDoc outbound, we support different options: either as message headers in the scenario-specific outbound processing flow, as externalized parameters for dedicated generic XI/Idoc outbound flows, or in the Partner Directory. See XI Receiver Adapter and IDoc Receiver Adapter.

In our case, we use the Partner Directory option. For the Partner Directory option, some of the parameters can be configured for the partner ID representing the configuration scenario or for the partner ID representing the party. In the configuration scenario, you then need to add the combined party and system alias as well as the receiver interface name as suffix to the parameter, e.g., XIAuthenticationType_PRTY_02L_Copper.BC_02L_R1_SI_PurchaseOrderCreatePD_IB_Async. For the parameter InterfaceNameDetermination, it's just the combined party and system alias, e.g., InterfaceNameDetermination_PRTY_02L_Copper.BC_02L_R1.

If you like to maintain party-specific parameters, create a new partner ID with name equals the party name, here PRTY_02L_Copper and PRTY_02L_Bronze. For the parties, you need to add the business system name and not the alias as suffix to the parameter, e.g., XIEndpoint_BS_02L_R1Q.

I switched on the trace for the generic XI outbound processing flow. In the trace, you can see the payload of the outgoing message including XI header. So, here you can see that the XI header contains the receiver party PRTY_02L_Copper and the receiver service BS_02L_R1Q.

To fetch the scenario and connection parameters both are read, the configuration scenario and the party. As you can see, the correct values were read and the message could be successful delivered.

XI/IDoc Outbound without staging

Now, let's check how you could configure XI and IDoc outbound without staging if this is not required. So, we distinguish between two parties but use a business component as receiver system. In this case, you do not need to define a business alias, you simply use the business component name in the configuration, here EDI.

For the party, we also add the business component as suffix to the parameter.

For a complete list of parameters that you can define in both the configuration scenario and the party, refer to XI Receiver Adapter and IDoc Receiver Adapter.
