entry.title: BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent | Part 3: Second Content Agent and target in Central
entry.content:
Part 3 of the series BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent.

In Part 2 we set up Dev, so a parcel can now be packed and dropped at the source node. In this part we build the receiving end in Central: a second Content Agent that unpacks the parcel, the connection CTMS uses to reach it, and the connection it uses to write into the target Integration Suite.

 

Before you start

The target Integration Suite runs in Central, with the Cloud Integration capability activated (the same rule as in Dev).

Step 1: Process Integration Runtime instance and key

Same as in Dev: an instance of SAP Process Integration Runtime, plan api, with the roles WorkspacePackagesRead, WorkspacePackagesEdit and WorkspacePackagesTransport, and a service key. This time it gives the unpacker access to the target workspace.

Step 2: The second Content Agent

  • Create an instance of Content Agent service with the application plan and the role Import. This is the unpacker.
  • Create a service key. You need its url and, from the uaa section, clientid, clientsecret and url.

Step 3: CloudIntegration destination in Central

The unpacker writes into Integration Suite through a destination named CloudIntegration, filled exactly like the Dev one in Part 2, but from the key of step 1. You can also let the Content Agent UI create it for you when you activate the Cloud Integration content type (see "What tripped me up" first).

Step 4: The transport destination CTMS uses

CTMS needs to know where to deliver the parcel. In Central, create a destination for that. Its name is free; I used CAS_on_target.

FieldValue
URLurl from the Content Agent key (step 2)
AuthenticationOAuth2ClientCredentials
Client ID / secretclientid / clientsecret from the uaa section
Token Service URLurl from the uaa section + /oauth/token

Step 5: Finish the target node

Open CTMS, edit the target node from Part 1 and pick CAS_on_target as its destination. The content type stays Multi-Target Application.

 

The target node with its content type and destination.

A green Check Connection on CAS_on_target only proves the address is reachable (Part 2 explains why). The real test is the first transport in Part 4.

What tripped me up in my setup

  • Three identical runtime instances. Central had three Process Integration Runtime instances with the same name, each in a different Cloud Foundry space, left over from earlier attempts. Before copying a key I had to check which space the target Cloud Integration actually runs in, and use the instance from that space. Clear names would have saved me this.
  • Activating the content type failed because the destination already existed. Activating the Cloud Integration content type in the Content Agent UI creates a CloudIntegration destination for you. I had already created one by hand, so the activation did not go through. It also asks for a Cloud Foundry passcode, and I first suspected the login URL and changed it to the Cloud Foundry API endpoint, which changed nothing. The fix was simple: I edited my existing CloudIntegration destination, added the client secret, and the activation went through. Either create the destination by hand or let the Content Agent UI do it, not both.

Roles for this part

Instance roles only: the three Workspace roles on the runtime instance and Import on the Content Agent instance. The user roles come in Part 4, and Part 7 lists them all.

What comes next

Both ends are now connected. In Part 4 we switch on Transport in Integration Suite, send the first package and import it in CTMS, including the role that kept the Transport option greyed out for me.

entry.title: Consuming SAP Integration Suite OData Provisioning from SAP Business Application Studio Across BTP
entry.content:
SAP OData Provisioning with BAS / SAP Fiori Tools Across BTP Subaccounts

Step 1: Configure the Backend Connection for OData Provisioning

In the SAP Integration Suite subaccount, create an HTTP destination pointing to the SAP Business Suite backend.

A simplified destination configuration is:

Name: ECC_ODP_BACKEND

Type: HTTP

ProxyType: OnPremise

Authentication: PrincipalPropagation

sap-client: 100

odc: true

Backend URL: SAP Backend Example

The important OData Provisioning property is:

odc = true

This destination provides the connection from OData Provisioning to the on-premise SAP backend.

Step 2: Register the OData Service

In SAP Integration Suite, navigate to:

Configure

→ OData Services

→ Register

Select the backend destination created in Step 1.

Then register the required OData service.

For example:

ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV

After registration, the service is published through OData Provisioning rather than being consumed directly from the on-premise SAP Gateway endpoint.

Step 3: Create OData Provisioning Runtime Access

For runtime access, create the appropriate OData Provisioning runtime service instance and service key.

The generated credentials conceptually contain the following information:

API URL:

ODP Runtime Host.<region>.hana.ondemand.com

Client ID:

sb-dummy-client-id

Client Secret:

dummy-client-secret

Grant Type:

client_credentials

Token URL:

Authentication Host.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/oauth/token

The configuration discussed here uses:

Service: xfs-runtime

Plan: odpruntime

The service-key credentials provide the information needed to authenticate against the OData Provisioning runtime.

Step 4: Test OAuth Independently from BAS

Before configuring SAP Fiori Tools, first verify the ODP runtime independently from the BAS terminal.

Obtain an OAuth access token using the Client ID and Client Secret.

Example command:

curl -s \

-X POST \

-u 'sb-dummy-client-id:dummy-client-secret' \

-H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \

-d 'grant_type=client_credentials' \

'ODP OAuth Token Endpoint'

After receiving the token, save it locally:

export TOKEN='<access-token>'

This test is useful because it validates OAuth authentication separately from the SAP Fiori Tools configuration.

Step 5: Use the Correct ODP Runtime Endpoint

This was one of the key findings during troubleshooting.

Initially, the Integration Suite application URL was tested using a URL similar to:

https://<tenant>.integrationsuite.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/xfsrt/odp/...

An unauthenticated curl request returned:

HTTP 200

However, the returned content was:

Content-Type: text/html

The response contained an interactive XSUAA login flow rather than an OData response.

Therefore, an important troubleshooting rule is:

HTTP 200 does not automatically mean that the OData request succeeded.

The correct test in this setup is against the ODP runtime host supplied by the runtime credentials.

Example:

ODP Runtime Endpoint

Step 6: Validate an Individual OData Service

The working ODP service URL follows this structure:

https://services.odp.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/odata/SAP/<SERVICE>;v=<VERSION>/

For example:

ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV

To retrieve the service metadata, execute:

curl -sk \

-H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \

-H "Accept: application/xml" \

"ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV Metadata"

A successful result should return:

HTTP 200 OK

and:

Content-Type: application/xml

The metadata should begin with an XML element similar to:

<edmx:Edmx ...>

At this stage, the test independently validates:

  • BAS network connectivity: OK
  • OAuth token acquisition: OK
  • ODP runtime authentication: OK
  • Registered OData service: OK
  • OData metadata retrieval: OK

Step 7: Validate the OData Provisioning Service Catalog

Another important finding is that OData Provisioning exposes its own CATALOGSERVICE.

The catalog metadata can be tested using:

curl -sk \

-H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \

-H "Accept: application/xml" \

"https://services.odp.cfapps.eu10.hana.ondemand.com/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2/$metadata"

The catalog contains entities such as:

  • ServiceCollection
  • CatalogCollection
  • Annotations
  • Vocabularies
  • TagCollection
  • EntitySetCollection

To retrieve the registered OData services:

curl -sk \

-H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \

-H "Accept: application/json" \

'ODP Service Collection'

For a registered service such as ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV, the response contains information conceptually similar to:

Description: Project Request

Title: ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV

TechnicalServiceName: ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV

TechnicalServiceVersion: 1

Service URL: ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV

Metadata URL: ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV Metadata

This proves independently that the ODP catalog itself is working correctly.

Step 8: Configure the BAS / Build Code Subaccount Destination

In the BAS / Build Code subaccount, create the following destination.

Name: SAP_Gateway

Type: HTTP

URL: ODP Runtime Host

ProxyType: Internet

Authentication: OAuth2ClientCredentials

Client ID: sb-dummy-client-id

Client Secret: dummy-client-secret

Token Service URL: ODP OAuth Token Endpoint

Add the following additional properties:

WebIDEEnabled: true

WebIDEUsage: odata_gen

HTML5.DynamicDestination: true

HTML5.Timeout: 60000

Important

Do not add $metadata to the destination URL.

The destination should point to the ODP runtime host.

Understanding WebIDEUsage

Understanding WebIDEUsage became one of the most important parts of the troubleshooting.

WebIDEUsage = odata_gen

With:

WebIDEUsage = odata_gen

SAP Fiori Tools treats the destination as a generic/partial OData destination in the tested setup.

In the Fiori Application Generator, select:

Connect to a System

→ SAP_Gateway

BAS then presents a Service Path field.

Enter the required ODP service path.

For example:

/odata/SAP/ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV;v=1/

This works in the tested environment.

The configuration is therefore effectively:

ODP Runtime Host

  •  

OData Service Path

=

Complete OData Service URL

For example:

ODP Runtime Host:

services.odp.cfapps.eu10.hana.ondemand.com

Service Path:

/odata/SAP/ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV;v=1/

Why odata_abap Fails with OData Provisioning

Initially, the expectation was that:

WebIDEUsage = odata_abap

would allow BAS / SAP Fiori Tools to display and browse the ODP catalog automatically.

Instead, BAS returned:

Internal server error

Request failed with status code 500

Running:

Fiori: Open Environment Check

revealed the actual problem.

For OData V2 catalog discovery, Fiori Tools constructed:

/sap/opu/odata/IWFND/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

For OData V4, it attempted:

/sap/opu/odata4/iwfnd/config/default/iwfnd/catalog/0002

These are ABAP Gateway catalog routes.

However, the working OData Provisioning catalog in this environment is:

/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

Therefore, there is a catalog-path mismatch.

OData Provisioning

Catalog Path:

/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

Result: OK

BAS with odata_abap

Catalog Path attempted by Fiori Tools:

/sap/opu/odata/IWFND/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

Result: FAIL

This means the observed issue was not caused by OAuth authentication.

It was not caused by Cloud Connector connectivity.

It was not caused by ODP service registration.

It was not caused by the ODP runtime itself.

The problem was the difference between the catalog URL exposed by OData Provisioning and the standard ABAP Gateway catalog URL expected by the odata_abap discovery flow.

What About odata_hcp_odp?

Older SAP Web IDE documentation contains another WebIDEUsage value:

WebIDEUsage = odata_hcp_odp

Historically, the distinction was:

odata_abap

for OData services hosted on SAP Gateway systems.

Whereas:

odata_hcp_odp

was associated with OData Provisioning systems on SAP Cloud Platform.

This initially appeared to match the required architecture.

However, in the tested current BAS/Fiori Tools environment, after configuring:

WebIDEUsage = odata_hcp_odp

the destination was not displayed in the Fiori Application Generator.

The observed behavior was therefore:

odata_gen

Destination visible

→ Service Path field available

→ ODP service path can be entered

→ Works

odata_abap

Destination visible

→ Standard ABAP catalog attempted

→ Catalog discovery fails

odata_hcp_odp

Destination not displayed in the tested Fiori Application Generator

Current Working Approach

For the tested BAS/Fiori Tools environment, the reliable configuration was:

URL: services.odp.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com

Authentication: OAuth2ClientCredentials

WebIDEUsage: odata_gen

WebIDEEnabled: true

HTML5.DynamicDestination: true

HTML5.Timeout: 60000

Developers then select:

Connect to a System

↓

SAP_Gateway

↓

Service Path

and enter:

/odata/SAP/<SERVICE>;v=<VERSION>/

For example:

/odata/SAP/ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV;v=1/

Catalog Browsing Limitation

The ODP catalog itself is operational.

The registered services can be retrieved from:

/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2/ServiceCollection

However, in the tested BAS/Fiori Tools environment, the native Connect to a System → catalog selection flow could not consume the ODP catalog in the same way.

The important distinction is:

OData Provisioning Flow

ODP

↓

/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

↓

Direct OAuth request works

↓

ServiceCollection

↓

ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV

BAS odata_abap Flow

BAS / Fiori Tools

↓

WebIDEUsage = odata_abap

↓

/sap/opu/odata/IWFND/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

↓

Fails because a different catalog path is being requested

If the catalog-selection UX is mandatory, support for an ODP-specific discovery mechanism should be validated for the target SAP Fiori Tools environment.

Principal Propagation and End-User Identity

There is another important distinction between design-time authentication and runtime end-user identity propagation.

OAuth2ClientCredentials is useful in this scenario for:

  • Design-time connectivity
  • Verifying the ODP runtime
  • Retrieving the ODP catalog
  • Retrieving OData metadata
  • Testing the OData service from BAS

However, Client Credentials represents the OAuth client, not the interactive Fiori end user.

If the runtime requirement is:

User A logs into Fiori

↓

Request reaches ABAP

↓

sy-uname = USER_A

and:

User B logs into Fiori

↓

Request reaches ABAP

↓

sy-uname = USER_B

then the runtime architecture must preserve the user context rather than relying solely on the Client Credentials token.

In the described landscape, the downstream configuration was:

OData Provisioning

↓

Principal Propagation Destination

↓

SAP Cloud Connector

↓

ABAP Backend

When accessed using the required interactive user context, the mapped SAP user was received in the ABAP backend through:

sy-uname

Therefore, BAS design-time authentication and runtime end-user principal propagation should be treated as separate concerns.

Troubleshooting Checklist

1. Check Network Connectivity

Verify that BAS can reach the ODP runtime host:

services.odp.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com

If this fails, troubleshoot network connectivity before investigating the Fiori Tools configuration.

2. Check OAuth Authentication

Verify that the ODP runtime service credentials can generate an OAuth access token.

Confirm that the following are correct:

  • Client ID
  • Client Secret
  • Grant Type
  • Token Service URL

The expected grant type in this setup is:

client_credentials

3. Check the Individual ODP Service

Using the OAuth token, retrieve:

/odata/SAP/<SERVICE>;v=<VERSION>/$metadata

For example:

/odata/SAP/ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV;v=1/$metadata

A successful response should return:

HTTP 200 OK

and XML metadata.

4. Check the ODP Catalog

Using the same OAuth token, verify:

/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2/$metadata

Then verify:

/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2/ServiceCollection?$format=json

If both requests succeed, the ODP catalog itself is operational.

5. Run BAS Environment Check

In BAS, run:

Fiori: Open Environment Check

This was particularly useful because it exposed the catalog URL that Fiori Tools was actually requesting.

In this case, it showed:

/sap/opu/odata/IWFND/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

rather than the working ODP catalog path:

/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

6. Always Inspect the Response Content Type

A common troubleshooting mistake is assuming:

HTTP 200 = OData request succeeded

That is not necessarily true.

For $metadata, expect an XML response such as:

Content-Type: application/xml

The response should contain metadata beginning with something similar to:

<edmx:Edmx>

If the response instead contains:

Content-Type: text/html

the request may have returned an authentication or login page rather than OData metadata.

Final Validation Result

The tested setup produced the following results:

✅ BAS → ODP network connectivity: WORKING

✅ ODP OAuth runtime access: WORKING

✅ ODP service metadata: WORKING

✅ ODP CATALOGSERVICE: WORKING

✅ ODP ServiceCollection: WORKING

✅ ODP → ABAP Principal Propagation: WORKING

✅ odata_gen + Service Path: WORKING

❌ odata_abap automatic catalog browsing: NOT WORKING

⚠️ Historical odata_hcp_odp: Destination not displayed in the tested current Fiori Application Generator

Conclusion

The most important lesson from this troubleshooting exercise is to separate four different layers:

1. BAS → ODP Network Connectivity

2. BAS → ODP Authentication

3. Fiori Tools Design-Time Service Discovery

4. ODP → SAP Backend Principal Propagation

In this case, network connectivity worked.

OAuth runtime authentication worked.

Individual OData service metadata worked.

The ODP CATALOGSERVICE worked.

The ODP ServiceCollection worked.

Principal Propagation from ODP to the ABAP backend worked.

The remaining problem was specifically the design-time catalog-discovery mechanism used by Fiori Tools with odata_abap.

The working development approach in the tested environment was therefore:

SAP Integration Suite

↓

OData Provisioning

↓

xfs-runtime OAuth Credentials

↓

BAS Destination

↓

WebIDEUsage = odata_gen

↓

Connect to a System

↓

SAP_Gateway

↓

Service Path

↓

/odata/SAP/<SERVICE>;v=<VERSION>/

For example:

/odata/SAP/ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV;v=1/

This approach keeps the SAP Integration Suite OData Provisioning runtime separate from the underlying SAP Gateway implementation and provides the working path used in this cross-subaccount setup.

entry.title: SAP S/4HANA Outbound IDoc Integration With SAP CPI: Complete Configuration Guide
entry.content:
Introduction

Many integration scenarios require SAP S/4HANA to send master or transactional data to external systems. IDocs are a standard way to do this, and SAP Cloud Integration (SAP CPI) can receive them over HTTPS. Setting this up involves several connected pieces: a logical system, an RFC destination, an XML HTTP port, a partner profile, and a distribution model. Missing any one of them causes errors that can be hard to trace.

In this blog, I walk through the complete outbound IDoc configuration from SAP S/4HANA 2023 to SAP Cloud Integration, using MATMAS as the example. You will see how to configure each component, test the connection, trigger an IDoc, and monitor it on both the SAP and CPI sides. This blog is useful for SAP integration consultants and developers who are new to IDoc-to-CPI connectivity.

Complete Guide to SAP S/4HANA Outbound IDoc Configuration with SAP Cloud Integration (SAP CPI)


Prerequisites

  • SAP S/4HANA 2023
  • SAP Integration Suite
  • SAP GUI
  • Authorization for ALE configuration
  • Deployed CPI iFlow
  • Service Key
  • SSL Certificates

 End-to-End Integration Flow: SAP S/4HANA to SAP Cloud Integration

The following diagram illustrates the end-to-end communication flow of an outbound IDoc from SAP S/4HANA to SAP Cloud Integration, highlighting the key SAP components involved in secure IDoc transmission.

Configuration Steps

 


Configure the Logical System :
Step : 1
       You can create a logical system either by using transaction SALE or directly through BD54. If you use SALE, navigate to Basic Settings → Logical Systems → Define Logical System. This opens the same configuration screen as transaction BD54.


In the Define Logical System screen, click New Entries, create a logical system by providing a unique Logical System Name and a meaningful Description, and then save the configuration.


The logical system uniquely identifies the sender (SAP S/4HANA) and the receiver (SAP Cloud Integration) during ALE/IDoc communication and is required for successful outbound IDoc processing.

Create the Integration Flow in SAP Cloud Integration
Before configuring the RFC destination in SAP S/4HANA, create and deploy an Integration Flow (iFlow) in SAP Cloud Integration.

Configure the Sender Adapter as an IDoc Adapter and maintain the required sender endpoint address. After deploying the iFlow, navigate to Monitor → Manage Integration Content, select the deployed integration flow, and copy the generated HTTPS endpoint URL. This endpoint will be used while configuring the RFC destination in SAP S/4HANA.

    Note: For security reasons, the tenant host name shown in the screenshots has been blurred.



Importing the SAP Cloud Integration SSL Certificate into SAP S/4HANA (STRUST)Before SAP S/4HANA can securely communicate with SAP Cloud Integration (SAP CPI) over HTTPS, the SSL certificates of your SAP Integration Suite tenant must be imported into the SAP Trust Manager (STRUST). This establishes a trusted SSL connection and prevents certificate validation errors during IDoc transmission.

Step 1: Export the SAP Integration Suite Certificates

  1. Open your deployed SAP Cloud Integration iFlow URL in your web browser.
  2. Click the View Site Information (🔒 Lock icon) beside the URL.
  3. Select Connection is secure.
  4. Click Certificate is valid.
  5. Open the Details tab.
  6. Under Certificate Hierarchy, export the following three certificates individually:
  • DigiCert TLS RSA4096 Root G5
  • DigiCert G5 TLS RSA4096 SHA384 2021 CA1
  • *.it-cpitrial03.cfapps.ap21.hana.ondemand.com (Your SAP Integration Suite tenant certificate)

Note: Save all three certificates in a local folder. These certificates establish the complete trust chain required for secure HTTPS communication.
Step 2: Copy the Certificates to the SAP Server

Copy the exported certificate files to the SAP application server (or a location accessible from SAP GUI). This allows SAP to import the certificates into its Trust Manager.


Step 3: Import the Certificates in STRUST

  1. Execute transaction STRUST.
  2. Expand SSL Client (Anonymous) (or the SSL Client PSE used by your RFC destination).
  3. Click Import Certificate.
  4. Browse to the folder where the certificates are stored.
  5. Select one certificate and click Continue.
  6. If prompted with the SAP GUI Security dialog, click Allow to grant access to the selected file.
  7. Repeat the same process for all three certificates.
  8. After importing all certificates, click Add to Certificate List and Save the changes.

Important: Import the certificates in the same order as shown in the certificate hierarchy (Root CA → Intermediate CA → SAP Integration Suite Tenant Certificate). This ensures the complete certificate chain is trusted by SAP.

Why is STRUST Configuration Required?
STRUST is used to establish trust between SAP S/4HANA and external HTTPS systems. Since SAP Cloud Integration communicates over SSL/TLS, SAP S/4HANA must trust the server certificate presented by the SAP Integration Suite tenant. Without importing these certificates, the RFC destination may fail with SSL handshake or certificate validation errors.

Once the certificates are successfully imported, SAP S/4HANA can securely send outbound IDocs to SAP Cloud Integration through the configured XML HTTP Port and RFC destination.

Create the RFC Destination
What is an RFC Destination?

An RFC (Remote Function Call) an RFC Destination defines the communication settings that allow SAP S/4HANA to connect to external systems. In this scenario, it enables SAP S/4HANA to securely send outbound IDocs to SAP Cloud Integration over HTTPS.

You can create the RFC destination either by navigating through the SALE transaction or directly using SM59.
If you use SALE, navigate to:

Basic Settings → Communication → Create RFC Connections

This option opens the same configuration screen as transaction SM59, where you can create the HTTP RFC destination.

The Configuration of RFC Connections screen displays various types of RFC destinations that can be used to communicate with different systems. For communication between SAP S/4HANA and SAP Cloud Integration (SAP CPI), select HTTP Connections to External Server, as SAP CPI is accessed through an HTTPS endpoint.

To create a new RFC destination, select HTTP Connections to External Server and click Create, as shown in the figure below.

In the Create Destination dialog, enter a meaningful destination name (for example, RFC_JD_CPI) and select G – HTTP Connection to External Server as the Connection Type. The appearance of this dialog may vary slightly depending on your SAP S/4HANA release, but the required Connection Type (G) remains the same.

After choosing the destination name and connection type, click the Continue (✔) button to create the RFC destination. In the next step, configure the Technical Settings, Logon & Security, and SSL parameters using the SAP CPI endpoint and SAP BTP credentials obtained from the deployed integration flow.

  Note: The screenshots in this blog are based on SAP S/4HANA 2023. Depending on your SAP release, the screen layout may differ slightly; however, the configuration steps and required settings remain the same.

Configure the RFC Destination
After creating the RFC destination, maintain the required connection details in the Technical Settings and Logon & Security tabs.

Technical Settings

Open the Technical Settings tab and maintain the following information:

  • Description – Provide a meaningful description for the RFC destination (for example, Secure communication from SAP S/4HANA to SAP Cloud Integration).
  • Host – Enter the SAP Cloud Integration tenant host name copied from the deployed iFlow endpoint.
  • Port – Specify 443 for secure HTTPS communication.
  • Path Prefix – Enter only the endpoint path generated by the deployed iFlow (for example, /cxf/JD/klaus/out).

Note: The endpoint URL displayed in Monitor → Manage Integration Content consists of the Host and Path Prefix. In the RFC destination, enter the Host and Path Prefix in their respective fields instead of pasting the complete URL.

Logon & Security

Next, navigate to the Logon & Security tab.

Under Logon Procedure, select Basic Authentication and maintain the authentication credentials for SAP Cloud Integration. It is highly recommended to use the Client ID and Client Secret obtained from the SAP Integration Suite Standard Service Key, as this is the recommended authentication method for production environments. Alternatively, for development or testing purposes, you can authenticate using your SAP Cloud Integration tenant user ID and password. If you are unsure how to obtain these credentials, refer to the SAP documentation using the link provided below.


After entering the credentials, scroll down to the Security Options section.

Enable SSL by changing the status from Inactive to Active. For the SSL Client PSE, select either:

  • DEFAULT SSL Client (Standard) (recommended), or
  • Anonymous SSL Client, depending on your organization's security requirements.

This configuration enables secure HTTPS communication between SAP S/4HANA and SAP Cloud Integration.

Test the Connection

After saving the RFC destination, execute the Connection Test to verify that SAP S/4HANA can reach the SAP Cloud Integration endpoint.

When testing an IDoc Sender Adapter, receiving an HTTP Response Status 500 (Internal Server Error) is generally expected. The IDoc sender endpoint is designed to process IDoc requests and does not respond to a simple HTTP GET request issued by the connection test.

The important point is that the connection successfully reaches the SAP Cloud Integration tenant, confirming that:

  • The Host, Port, and Path Prefix are configured correctly.
  • SSL communication is established successfully.
  • SAP S/4HANA can communicate with the SAP Cloud Integration tenant.



    Examples:
  • HTTP 401 – Invalid authentication credentials.
  • HTTP 403 – Authorization issue.
  • HTTP 500 – Connection established; check the CPI iFlow and endpoint.
  • SSLHandshakeException – Certificate not imported in STRUST.

No communication IDoc generated – Verify Partner Profile, Distribution Model, Logical System, and Message Type.

Create an XML HTTP Port (WE21)

The next step is to create an XML HTTP Port, which is used to route outbound IDocs from SAP S/4HANA to SAP Cloud Integration (SAP CPI) through the configured RFC destination.

Navigate to transaction WE21. In the Ports tree, expand XML HTTP and click the Create icon (or press F7) to create a new XML HTTP port.

Enter a meaningful Port name (for example, PORT_JD_CI) and maintain an appropriate Description. In the RFC Destination field, enter the RFC destination created in the previous step (for example, RFC_JD_CPI).

For the remaining settings:

  • Set the Content Type to application/x-sap.idoc.
  • Select the SOAP Protocol checkbox.
  • Leave the remaining settings with their default values unless your project requires additional configuration.

After maintaining all the required fields, save the XML HTTP port.

This XML HTTP port is now linked to the RFC destination and will be assigned to the outbound partner profile in WE20. During IDoc processing, SAP uses this port to transmit outbound IDocs securely to the SAP Cloud Integration endpoint.


Create the Partner Profile (WE20)

A partner profile defines how IDocs are exchanged between the sender and receiver systems. It contains the communication settings required for outbound and inbound IDoc processing, such as the partner, message type, port, and IDoc type.

Navigate to transaction WE20 to create the partner profile. Under Partner Type, select LS (Logical System) and create a new partner profile.



Maintain the following details:

  • Partner No. – Enter the Logical System name created earlier in BD54 (for example, JD_SAP_CPI).
  • Partner Type – Select LS (Logical System).

Next, under the Post Processing: Valid Processors tab, maintain the following:

Type – Select the appropriate processor type based on your requirement. In this example, US (User) is selected.
Agent – Enter the corresponding processor value. In this example, the SAP user ID is maintained as the Agent.
Language – Set the language to EN (English).
After maintaining these details, save the partner profile. In the next step, configure the Outbound Parameters by assigning the required Message Type, Receiver Port, and Basic Type for outbound IDoc communication.

Configure Outbound Parameters (WE20)

After saving the partner profile, the next step is to configure the Outbound Parameters. In the Outbound section, click the Add icon (highlighted in the screenshot) to create a new outbound parameter for the partner profile.



Maintain the following details:

  • Message Type – Enter the required message type (for example, MATMAS).
  • Receiver Port – Select the XML HTTP port created earlier in WE21 (for example, PORT_JD_CI).
  • Output Mode – Select Pass IDoc Immediately to transmit the IDoc as soon as it is generated.
  • Basic Type – Select the IDoc basic type that corresponds to your integration scenario (for example, MATMAS07).

After maintaining the required fields, save the outbound parameter configuration.

Message Type identifies the business message being exchanged between systems, such as MATMAS for Material Master or DEBMAS for Customer Master.

Basic Type defines the IDoc structure, including its segments and fields, that is used to exchange the selected business message.

Configure the Distribution Model (BD64)

The final ALE configuration step is to maintain the Distribution Model, which defines the sender, receiver, and message types that are allowed for IDoc distribution.

Navigate to transaction BD64, or use the following path in SALE:

SALE - Modeling and Implementing Business Processes → Maintain Distribution Model and Distribute Views




Open the Distribution Model and click the Change (Edit) icon. Next, choose Create Model View and enter a meaningful Short Text and Technical Name for your integration scenario (for example, JD_CPI_Idoc_Models). Save the model view.

After creating the model view, select it and click Add Message Type.

Maintain the following details:

  • Sender – Select the logical system of your SAP S/4HANA system.
  • Receiver – Select the receiver logical system created earlier in BD54 and used in WE20 (for example, JD_SAP_CPI).
  • Message Type – Select the same message type configured in the partner profile (for example, MATMAS).


    Save the configuration.

Note: A single distribution model can contain multiple message types. If your integration scenario requires sending different business objects (such as MATMAS, DEBMAS, CREMAS, or ORDERS), you can add multiple message types under the same model view. This enables SAP S/4HANA to route different outbound IDocs to the same receiver logical system.

Test the Outbound IDoc (WE19)

What is WE19?

WE19 is the SAP IDoc Test Tool, used to create, simulate, and trigger IDocs without executing an actual business transaction. It is commonly used to validate IDoc configurations and verify end-to-end communication between SAP S/4HANA and external systems such as SAP Cloud Integration (SAP CPI).

Use Case: WE19 is primarily used by developers and integration consultants to test IDoc interfaces, validate partner profile configurations, and troubleshoot integration issues before moving them to production.

Trigger the IDoc

Navigate to transaction WE19 and select Basic Type. Enter the required Message Type (for example, MATMAS) and click Execute.

In the IDoc structure, select the EDI_DC40 (EDIDC) control record and maintain the following details:

  • Receiver Port – XML HTTP Port created in WE21 (for example, PORT_JD_CI).
  • Receiver Partner No. – Logical System created for SAP CPI (for example, JD_SAP_CPI).
  • Receiver Partner Type – LS (Logical System).
  • Sender Port – SAP sender port.
  • Sender Partner No. – Sender logical system of SAP S/4HANA.
  • Sender Partner Type – LS (Logical System).
  • Message Type – MATMAS.


After maintaining the control record, save the changes and choose Standard Outbound Processing.

An Outbound Processing of IDoc dialog appears. Confirm the processing by clicking Continue. You will then receive the confirmation message "IDoc sent by HTTP in XML format". After successful processing, SAP displays the generated IDoc Number, confirming that the IDoc has been created and stored in the database.

Verify the Message in SAP Cloud Integration

Once the IDoc is triggered, navigate to Monitor → Message Processing in SAP Cloud Integration. You can verify that the IDoc has been received successfully.

As shown in the payload, the control record (EDI_DC40) contains the sender and receiver information configured earlier, including the Sender Logical System, Receiver Logical System, Receiver Port, Partner Type, and Message Type. This confirms that the configurations maintained in BD54, WE21, WE20, and BD64 have been applied successfully during IDoc processing.


Alternative Method to Trigger IDocs

In addition to WE19, IDocs can also be generated directly from business transactions.

  • BD10 – Trigger Material Master (MATMAS) IDocs.
  • BD12 – Trigger Customer Master (DEBMAS) IDocs.

These transactions generate IDocs from actual master data records instead of creating a test IDoc. Simply select the required material or customer record, specify the appropriate Message Type, and execute the transaction. SAP automatically creates and sends the IDoc using the configured Partner Profile, Port, and Distribution Model.

Note: WE19 is ideal for interface testing and troubleshooting, whereas BD10 and BD12 are typically used to send actual business master data to the target system.

Trigger Material Master IDoc Using BD10

BD10 is used to generate and send Material Master (MATMAS) IDocs from SAP S/4HANA to external systems. Unlike WE19, which is mainly used for testing, BD10 sends IDocs based on actual material master data maintained in SAP.

Execute transaction BD10 and enter the following details:

  • Material – Enter a valid Material Number.
  • Message Type – Enter MATMAS.
  • Logical System – Enter the receiver logical system created in BD54 (for example, JD_SAP_CPI).

Note: Ensure that the material number is valid and maintained in SAP. If the material does not exist or the logical system/message type is configured incorrectly, the IDoc will not be generated.


Click Execute. A confirmation popup appears stating "1 master IDoc set up for message type MATMAS." Click Continue



A second confirmation popup displays "1 communication IDoc(s) generated for message type MATMAS." Click Continue again. SAP then generates the IDoc and sends it to SAP Cloud Integration (SAP CPI) using the configured Partner Profile, XML HTTP Port, and Distribution Model.



If the popup displays 0 communication IDoc(s), no IDoc has been generated. In this case, verify that the Material Number, Message Type, and Logical System are configured correctly.

Similarly, to trigger Customer Master IDocs, use transaction BD12, enter the required customer details, Message Type, and Logical System, and execute the transaction. The process is the same as BD10.

Monitor IDoc Status (WE02)

After triggering the IDoc using WE19, BD10, or BD12, you can monitor its processing status using transaction WE02 (IDoc Display). This transaction provides detailed information about generated IDocs, including the IDoc number, Message Type, Basic Type, Partner, Port, Direction, Processing Status, and error details.

In the screenshot below, multiple outbound MATMAS IDocs are displayed with different processing statuses.


Common Outbound IDoc Status Codes

Status

Description

30

IDoc ready for dispatch. The IDoc has been created successfully and is waiting to be sent to the configured port.

03

Data passed to port successfully. The IDoc was successfully sent to the configured XML HTTP Port and forwarded to SAP Cloud Integration (SAP CPI). This indicates successful outbound processing.

02

Error passing data to port. The IDoc could not be sent due to a communication or configuration issue, such as an incorrect RFC Destination, SSL configuration, authentication, or network problem. Open the IDoc to view the detailed error message.

29

Error in ALE service. An error occurred during ALE processing before the IDoc could be sent. Verify the Partner Profile, Distribution Model, Logical System, and Port configuration.

32

IDoc was passed to the application successfully. This status is mainly seen for inbound processing, indicating that the receiving application processed the IDoc successfully.

51

Application document not posted. The IDoc reached the receiving application, but processing failed due to business or application errors. This status is commonly seen for inbound IDocs.

53

Application document posted successfully. The IDoc was processed successfully, and the business document was created. This status is commonly seen for inbound IDocs.

Note: For outbound IDocs sent from SAP S/4HANA to SAP CPI, the most commonly encountered status codes are 30, 03, and 02.

Conclusion

In this blog, we configured an end-to-end outbound IDoc integration from SAP S/4HANA to SAP Cloud Integration using MATMAS as the example. We created the RFC Destination, XML HTTP Port, Partner Profile and Distribution Model, and then triggered and monitored the IDoc using WE19 and BD10. The same approach can be extended to other message types such as DEBMAS, CREMAS, ORDERS and INVOIC with minimal configuration changes.

I hope this guide helps you set up your own outbound IDoc scenarios. If you have questions or run into issues, please leave a comment below. I’d also encourage you to follow the SAP Integration Suite and SAP S/4HANA tags for related content.

entry.title: From Integration to Intelligence :Building enterprise-ready AI agents with Integration Suite & MCP
entry.content:
I have sat through a lot of agent demos this year. The pattern is usually the same. Someone types a request in plain English, the agent reads a purchase requisition, checks a budget, creates a purchase order in S/4HANA, emails the supplier, and posts a cheerful summary. The room claps. It is impressive.

Then I ask the question that integration people always ask: what happens on the 40,000th run? What happens when the supplier endpoint times out, when the mapping changes, when audit wants to know who approved what, or when the token bill arrives at the end of the month?

That is the gap between an agent that works in a demo and an agent that survives production. After close to two decades of building integrations, first on Oracle SOA and OSB, later on Boomi, Apigee and SAP BTP, my view is that the gap is mostly not a model problem. It is an architecture problem. And it is one the SAP integration community is unusually well placed to solve.

Last week I attended SAP's session "Building the Autonomous Enterprise with Integration Suite, AEM, and Agents" (13 October 2026). One line from it has stayed with me, because it captures the whole argument in eight words:

"Let the agent think. Let Integration Suite execute."

This post is my attempt to unpack that line from an architect's point of view: where agents earn their keep, where they should stay out of the way, and how API-centric integration and the MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite connect the two.

1. The overloaded agent

When teams first build agents, they tend to give them everything. The agent calls the APIs, builds the payloads, decides on retries, transforms the formats and handles the errors. It feels efficient because there is only one component to think about.

It is not efficient. In effect you are asking a probabilistic reasoning engine to re-implement things your integration platform already does deterministically, with monitoring, retries and audit built in. Mapping JSON to IDoc, routing a message by company code, validating mandatory fields against a schema, sending a payment file over a bank channel: none of these need judgment. They need to be done exactly the same way every time.

The SAP session framed the consequences well, and they match what I have seen in practice:

  • Duplicated capability. The agent rebuilds APIs, EDI handling, mappings and routing you already own.
  • Reduced reliability. Predictable PO, invoice and payment flows start to depend on non-deterministic behavior.
  • Harder governance. Security, auditability and compliance become difficult to standardize when logic lives inside prompts.
  • Blurred accountability. When something fails, is it the reasoning, the integration, the partner or the backend? Nobody can tell quickly.
  • Higher operating cost. Tokens and agent capacity are spent on repetitive plumbing instead of the reasoning you actually wanted.

I like to describe it as driving a Lamborghini to the supermarket. You can, but it is not what the car is for, and the parking is a nightmare.

2. Who should own each step? A Procure-to-Pay test

The most useful part of the session, for me, was a simple step-by-step assessment of a standard Procure-to-Pay flow. For each step, it asked one question: is the value here in reasoning, or in reliable execution? I have adapted it below because I think every team should run this exercise on its own processes before writing a single prompt.

#

P2P step

Integration Suite value

Agent value

Owner

Why

1

Create requisition

Low

Medium

Agent

Demand signals need interpretation

2

Approve requisition

Low

High

Agent

Summarize context and policy, recommend

3

Create purchase order

Very high

Low

Integration Suite

Structured execution: APIs, EDI, mapping

4

Supplier acknowledgement

Very high

Low

Integration Suite

Receive, transform, update

5

Goods receipt

Very high

Very low

Integration Suite

Synchronization, not decisions

6

Invoice processing

Very high

Low

Integration Suite

Standardized ingestion and routing

7

Three-way match

High

Medium

Shared

Match is deterministic; exceptions need reasoning

8

Invoice approval

Medium

High

Agent

Assemble evidence, justify a decision

9

Payment execution

Very high

Very low

Integration Suite

Must stay governed and deterministic

10
